workshops.title: Durable data lab: preserve old data and retry one saved command
workshops.summary: Run old-store migrations and a disk-backed retry after process restart. Then check synthetic sign-in failures and write a recovery plan with device work clearly marked.

simple.story: A bakery writes order 17 in its order book before sending it to the kitchen. The kitchen makes one loaf and records that order 17 is done. The reply is lost, so the front desk still sees a waiting order. After the desk closes and reopens, it sends order 17 again with the same details. The kitchen finds its saved receipt and reports the earlier result. It does not make a second loaf. The desk can now mark the order done.
simple.meaning: The outbox saves intent before delivery. The synthetic server saves an effect and its receipt together. If the reply is lost, the client keeps the command pending. A separate process retries the same immutable operation ID and payload, obtains the saved result, and persists acknowledgment.

example.before: For restart-account, stable-restart-op is saved with ambiguous delivery. The synthetic server has applied its value 'survives exit' once and saved the receipt. Pending count is 1; server effect count is 1.
example.change: After the seed process exits, run RestartProbe replay against the same directory so the new process resends stable-restart-op with its original payload.
example.after: The server returns the saved receipt without another effect. The client saves acknowledgment. Pending count becomes 0, and server effect count stays 1.

picture.caption: A lost reply leaves saved intent for a later process to retry under the same identity.

items.text: The client stores stable-restart-op before attempting delivery.

items.label: Effect, lost reply
items.text: The server saves one effect and its receipt, while the client keeps ambiguous intent.

words.meaning: Saved commands waiting to be delivered or acknowledged.
A saved result keyed to an operation identity so repeating that operation does not repeat its effect.
Changing a saved data format while preserving the intended old values.
An account activation number used to reject work from an earlier activation, even after returning to the same account.
Publishing one complete snapshot rather than a partially replaced file; it does not by itself prove power-loss durability.
Data whose access depends on the selected protection policy and device state.

simple.remember: Save the intent, retry the same operation, and acknowledge only after the saved result is known.
simple.boundary: The bakery story assumes a durable receipt with the effect. The lab uses a synthetic server, ordinary process exit, and atomic snapshots. It does not prove real-service receipt retention, abrupt-crash safety, fsync durability, or coordination between unrelated writers. Cancellation cannot undo a remote effect.

sections.title: Keep each kind of data check separate
sections.html:
A host check runs on the Mac. A device check runs where device services and protection rules apply. On Android, a JVM repository fake and an instrumentation migration test answer different questions; keep the same distinction here. This workbench uses Swift, Foundation, and Apple SDK frameworks. It has no remote packages, network calls, credentials, company capabilities, or client writes. Run the script from the companion directory. It creates a unique /private/tmp output root for caches and binaries and prints that path for your notes. Use its synthetic files, never a user's application database.

A journal is the saved local state used to recover work. The host checks exercise a JSON journal and synthetic server. CoreDataMigration creates a real old Core Data SQLite source and a distinct upgraded candidate. SwiftDataMigration creates a real disk store and reopens it with a versioned schema and plan. NativeChecks uses an in-memory Core Data store to verify context ownership. KeychainChecks constructs dictionaries and interprets statuses only. These rows must stay distinct even though one script orchestrates them.

Record compiler version, language mode, SDK path, command exit and assertions. The author used Apple Swift 6.4 in Swift 6 mode; exact commands and observed results are in README. The optional macro-helper flag addresses nested compiler sandbox initialization in this workspace; it does not change the outer workspace permission boundary. Successful host checks are available instruction, not learner completion or a production audit.

sections.title: Build an old store and compare every preserved value
sections.html:
A migration changes an old saved schema into a new one. A schema describes the stored fields and their rules. Read CoreDataMigration.swift from model construction through its final assertions. V1 seeds accounts A and B with identical IDs but different titles. It saves on a private context and removes the store from its coordinator. V2 adds a default and links displayTitle to the old title through migration identity. An inferred mapping tells NSMigrationManager how to convert this store into a candidate at a different URL. Compare the full account/ID/title/origin projection. Merely opening the candidate does not prove that values survived.

The failure checks supply an unsupported source model, invalid SQLite bytes, and a blocked destination parent. Each checks that original source bytes remain available. DELETE journaling simplifies this closed-file fixture; do not generalize its single-file comparison to copying a live WAL-backed client store. Cutover is intentionally outside the runnable fixture. A real replacement must exclude other writers, coordinate contexts and sidecars, and retain a compatible recovery path.

SwiftData uses its own schema and migration plan. SwiftDataMigration independently supplies V1/V2 VersionedSchema definitions and Plan. The old container explicitly saves before the new container opens the same URL. Attribute(originalName:) and the origin default preserve historical values. Its runtime assertions cover that particular path only. The author saw a store-notification registration diagnostic under the sandbox while the assertions passed, so extensions/cross-process notification behavior remains unverified. JSON decodeJournal verifies another format and cannot stand in for either framework migration.

sections.title: Lose a reply, exit, and retry from the saved files
sections.html:
An outbox stores commands that still need delivery or acknowledgment. Read DurableStore.swift before running RestartProbe. Its journal combines optimistic local records with pending commands. commit publishes new memory state only after one atomic snapshot write. Each operation keeps the same identity, payload, and base revision across attempts. A base revision names the server state the edit was prepared against. The synthetic server persists effects and idempotency receipts together. Those receipts are scoped by account and reject a changed payload under the same operation ID. This is local model evidence; no real service is contacted.

Ambiguous delivery means the client cannot tell from the reply whether the effect happened. RestartProbe seed writes a command, applies it at the synthetic server, intentionally loses the response, and saves that ambiguous state. That OS process exits. RestartProbe replay starts separately against the same directory, activates the account with a new epoch, reloads the pending command and server receipt, then persists acknowledgment. The asserted server effect count remains one. Use two invocations rather than claiming a newly constructed actor alone proves process restart.

Ordinary exit/restart demonstrates this controlled interval. It does not reproduce an abrupt kill during replacement, power loss, receipt expiry or real network behavior. Atomic writes also do not coordinate two unrelated writers for one path. The synchronous snapshot I/O is a bounded fixture on an actor's cooperative executor, with no fsync guarantee. Lesson 088 supplies the next production step: a bounded blocking-I/O worker whose result returns to a correctly ordered transaction owner.

sections.title: Keep unresolved commands when delivery or saving fails
sections.html:
A tombstone records a deletion so later stale edits do not silently bring the data back. HostChecks reloads commands, tests delete persistence, records conflict, and rejects an acknowledgment from an old A-to-B-to-A activation. A delete remains an explicit command after the local record disappears. The server retains a revision-bearing nil value as the deletion record. A conflict pauses the conservative account FIFO, which processes commands in queue order. The supplied scheduler does not merge or rebase automatically. Rebase means preparing a replacement edit against a newer known revision; that is the extension below.

RejectingDisk is a fake that fails before writing any new bytes. The host compares old bytes and same-actor state, proving preservation for that seam. setAvailable(false) similarly prevents a commit without erasing the old snapshot. Corrupt and unsupported envelopes retain their bytes and fail distinctly. Cancellation before enqueue preserves the prior file. If cancellation happens after a server effect, replayable intent must remain; a canceled UI task cannot establish server rollback.

A failure after the bytes were written has different consequences. A production adapter can write bytes and then fail protection/backup configuration. It must report incomplete policy enforcement rather than imply that the old file necessarily survived. Keep this later-step risk separate from the pre-write fake. Bounded diagnostics should describe outcome category and test identity rather than secret data, raw callback URLs or user-authored text. The exercise uses only synthetic evidence.

sections.title: Check token rotation when local storage fails
sections.html:
A refresh token lets a client ask for new credentials. Rotation replaces that token and can make the old one unusable at the provider. MockAuth checks this with synthetic values. It also checks one-time authorization codes, state validation, S256 verifier binding, credential installation, and logout. State links a response to the request; S256 binds the code exchange to a verifier through its SHA-256 challenge. The host checks a published S256 vector and rejects wrong or repeated state and reused codes. A result held across logout cannot install under the old epoch. FakeVault.save can fail while locked, and deletion can fail separately while local authorization stays closed and cleanup stays pending.

Follow this exact failure order: provider refresh rotation succeeds, then the vault rejects the new bytes. The current view still contains the old token, but that token was consumed remotely. Once unlocked, plain retry is denied; explicit reauthentication recovers. This mock has no reconciliation endpoint or grace window. A real provider can offer documented recovery, but a storage error does not create retry safety. Refresh here is single-caller, with no coalescing; the existing shared-refresh workbench is a conceptual companion rather than behavior implemented here.

The fixed verifier, state, and token strings make the synthetic checks repeatable. They are not production entropy, provider security or passkey support. KeychainChecks performs no SecItem calls, and the fake cleanup marker is memory-only. Actual browser ownership, provider interoperability, durable sign-out, signed Keychain availability and relying-party passkey verification require additional target/service evidence. Keep those gaps visible when reporting a passing script.

sections.title: Check context ownership and plan locked-device observations
sections.html:
A Core Data context owns access to its managed objects on its assigned queue. NativeTransactionOwner requires a dedicated main-queue context and a MainActor caller. Inside performAndWait, MainActor.assumeIsolated asserts that established bridge before checking the captured account/epoch and saving. That assertion does not move arbitrary work onto the main actor. NativeChecks runs against an in-memory macOS store, then reads through a fresh private context. The old A ticket fails after A-to-B-to-A, and B remains intact. A private context cannot use the same main-actor assertion; it needs a transaction owner for its own queue.

Protected data access depends on the file policy and current device state. ProtectedDataExercise has an iOS-only gate for UIApplication availability and complete-protection writing options. The script type-checks it for an iOS 17 deployment target against the installed iPhoneOS SDK. That establishes API compilation, not device file access. Plan a passcode-enabled scratch-device experiment with synthetic complete and completeUnlessOpen files, comparing retained-open and closed/reopened handles across lock/unlock. Observe actual operation errors even when an availability property suggested access.

Keychain stores items under identities such as service and account. Inspect this lab's synthetic query and the meanings of its status categories first. Keep any future signed adapter bounded to those identities and its own scratch target; no broad delete helper belongs in this workshop. Treat unavailable, absent, duplicate and configuration as separate outcomes. A durable bootstrap policy must consult sign-out obligations before reloading surviving credentials and granting outbox replay. The current lab supplies the fake/state seams and evidence boundaries, not that complete device implementation.

exercise.brief: In a scratch copy, add a historical optional field and one saved conflict-resolution command. Write a recovery handoff that separates observed checks from pending device and provider work.
steps: Run ValidateContent.py and run-checks.sh with a new temporary root. Record the compiler, SDK, and result of each check.
Add optional note to both Core Data models. Seed nil for A and text for B. Include both values in the preservation comparison.

Reproduce or extend resolveConflict independently. Replace one conflict in its original queue slot with a fresh-ID request. Reject multiple pending edits to that record unless one atomic policy reconciles their dependencies.
Make the resolution write fail before publication. Check that the original conflict and previously acknowledged local state remain unchanged.
Write a restart policy for durable sign-out and a locked/unlocked protected-file device matrix. Mark every row you have not executed.
acceptance: The old-store optional states and existing account/title/default values survive a real Core Data migration.
The conflict resolution uses a new identity/precondition and one durable local boundary.
A failed resolution write leaves the old command and memory/disk state intact.
The handoff includes separate-process replay, rotation/vault failure, native in-memory ownership and iOS type-check evidence.
Device protection, real Keychain/provider/passkeys, abrupt crash and cross-process writers are not claimed verified.
Conflict resolution preserves the original queue slot; unsupported same-record dependencies retain their bytes, order and preconditions.
exercise.solution:
Add the same optional note attribute to V1 and V2, with isOptional set to true. Seed text only for B, leaving A's note nil. Render nil with a distinct sentinel when comparing saved values. Check each account separately so an empty string cannot pass as absence. Keep the origin default and title rename as separate preservation checks. If the candidate fails the expanded comparison, reject it and leave the source untouched. This is how you test preservation of the old meaning, rather than only whether the new schema opens.

Independently reproduce the bounded resolveConflict command, then change its fixture. Validate the ticket, locate the marked conflict and reject more than one pending command for that record. Replace the entry at its original index with a fresh-ID request using the chosen value and supplied current revision; update the copied local record and persist the entire snapshot before changing journal. Preserve unrelated queue positions. Removing and appending would let a later edit to the same record execute first and invalidate the replacement precondition. A multi-edit resolver needs a separate atomic reconciliation design rather than deleting dependent intent implicitly.

The supplied HostChecks.rebaseChecks tests successful single-edit resolution, immutable historical receipts, failed-write preservation and a two-edit rejection. Change one expected ordering or add a second record to your independent exercise. Explain why dependentCommands preserves the old bytes and complete queue. Fetching the current server revision provides a snapshot, not a lock over the later replay; an intervening remote edit can legitimately cause another conflict.

For the failure assertion, instantiate a sequential replacement owner on RejectingDisk reading the existing acknowledged file. Attempt resolution, expect injectedDisk, compare before-image bytes, and read the still-conflicted queue through the same current ticket. For a successful rebase, use a separate writable fixture, replay with the new ID and verify one additional intended effect. Keep this separate from the original operation's receipt, which must continue returning its historical conflict.

The recovery handoff states that sign-out closes local authorization first, persists an obligation under a reviewed protection policy, attempts narrow vault cleanup, and gates restart credential loading until reconciliation. Marker-write and credential-delete failures each need an explicit owner and user-visible state. The fake vault cannot validate persistence of that policy. Attach the actual host exits and assertions, then label signed device lock tests, actual Keychain operations, browser/provider flows, receipt-retention negotiation and crash-at-cutover as pending. This worked answer shows the implementation boundary; your extension and acceptance record remain learner work.

quiz.question: Which result proves the separate-process outbox scenario?
options: A new actor reads an in-memory dictionary
seed exits, replay loads the same disk files, and the server effect count stays one
quiz.explanation: Two OS invocations and persisted intent/receipts exercise ordinary restart and idempotent replay. They still do not prove abrupt-crash or real-service semantics.

quiz.question: The provider rotated a token before the vault write failed. What does the mock demonstrate?
options: Unlock always makes the old token safe to retry
The failed write reverses provider rotation
Plain retry is denied; this provider requires explicit reauthentication
quiz.explanation: Storage failure cannot undo remote consumption. Reconciliation or grace requires a documented provider contract; this fake offers neither.

quiz.question: What does the iOS ProtectedDataExercise type-check establish?
options: The seam compiles against the stated SDK/target
A passcode device allowed locked access
A real Keychain item was deleted
quiz.explanation: Type-checking verifies source/API compatibility. Device protection and actual Security operations require separate runtime evidence.
